1:
The chapter has twenty-two verses, the number of letters in the alphabet, and is yet not alphabetic. Clarke calls the chapter a conclusion appended to the four before it, and supposes that anything so technical was not thought proper by men in agony asking for mercy. Ellicott infers the opposite, that the count of verses shows the chapter was meant to be alphabetic and that we have the last of the five elegies half finished; it would seem, he suggests, as if the prophet first wrote freely and then set to work as an artist to bring it under the scheme. Calvin takes the missing order as a reason to read the piece apart from the rest, and adds that it is a complaint rather than a prayer. Gill and Clarke both report that several versions head it as the prayer of the prophet, Clarke from an old manuscript Bible.

Gill records and rejects an allegorical reading that refers the whole to the church after the later destruction of the city; it is best, he holds, to understand it of the people in Babylon.

Henry takes the opening as a model of complaint. These give vent to their sorrows at the footstool of the throne of grace, and complain not of evils feared but of evils felt. It is a great comfort, and ought to be a sufficient one, that God sees and considers all that has come upon us. Calvin makes the same word do more work. The speech is fitted to human perception, since we imagine his back is turned whenever he does not succour us at once; he is simply to be asked to look, because as soon as he looks at the evils we suffer, help is prepared at the same moment.

Both dwell on the word reproach as the summary of the whole. Henry observes that the troubles were a greater reproach to this people than to any other, since they reflect on the name and honour of the God who had owned them. Calvin says the indignity is mentioned to move God the more, since he had taken them under his protection that they might be for his glory.

On the inheritance Calvin goes back to the promise, noting that the land had been promised four hundred years before the children possessed it; and he marks the escalation in the second clause, since a man may lose farm and fields and still keep his house, whereas these were ejected from their houses too, and he quotes an old poet who upbraided a great house for passing to an unequal master. Ellicott glosses the verb as transferred: since the invaders are said elsewhere to have burnt the houses of the city and of the great men, those here must belong to the farmers and peasants in the country.

The orphans and widows occasion the longest note. Keil and Delitzsch report that the verse is very variously interpreted, some taking the father for the king, while the mothers are made either the cities of Judah or the women of the royal harem; they answer that calling the harem mothers of the nation would be as unexampled as giving the title to the cities. Since the second clause is plainly a simile, the first must be a comparison too, and they connect it with the Hebrew custom of calling the utterly forsaken orphans and widows. Ellicott says the same, that the husbands though living were carried into exile. Gill takes the orphanage in every sense, natural, civil and religious, and Wesley the same, that they were without a king, and many children left without an earthly parent. Calvin observes that the prophet speaks not for the whole body but utters the groans of individuals, and that a country does not become full of orphans from one battle but from a vengeance continued until the people were spent.
4:
The force of the complaint about water and wood lies in the possessive pronouns. Ellicott says the point lies exactly there, since the conquerors held the country and the necessaries of life, once common property, were now to be had only for money. Keil and Delitzsch name the two as the greatest necessities of life, that what they formerly had as their own and for nothing they must now purchase. Calvin presses it further: the complaint is not that corn and wine were gone, but that water was sold, and the use of water is common to all, no man being so poor that he lacks enough to drink unless he lives in a dry land.

Keil and Delitzsch also reject a series of historical applications of the verse, to the distress of the besieged, to those who fled before the invaders, and to prisoners too closely watched to fetch either. Clarke illustrates the hardship from a countryman who never buys firewood at home but must purchase fuel in the city.

On the necks the readings differ. Keil and Delitzsch take it that the pursuers are at their necks, hold it inadmissible to supply any mention of a yoke, and reject the proposal to attach the phrase to the previous verse, since that destroys the symmetry and yields no suitable sense. Ellicott renders it that they were under pursuit, the enemy at their very heels. Clarke keeps the yoke, the bondage felt as by an ox driven to its work. Calvin turns the metaphor into a scale of insult: enemies may trouble us before our face, behind our backs or at our sides, but when they ride on our necks the degradation is extreme. He then makes it retribution, since the people had an iron neck, so that their enemies laid a burden there instead. Gill reports two readings, one taking it of a yoke and another connecting it with the water and wood, so that whatever they carried the enemy pursued them to take away.

Giving the hand is explained three ways, and Calvin lists them: humbly to ask, to make an agreement, or to hold it out in token of misery. He takes it simply of begging bread. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both make it the recognised gesture of submission, and Ellicott adds that hunger alone forced it. Calvin finds the sharpest disgrace in the choice of benefactors, since these had been their most troublesome enemies; and he sets it against the promise of a land so fertile that they were to lend and not borrow, so that begging bread was the evidence of an extreme curse.

The saying about the fathers is where all four fear the same misreading. Calvin says the prophet seems here to be repeating the proverb about the sour grape which another prophet condemns, and cites two Latin poets who blamed the crimes of ancestors and made their own generation wholly innocent. That, he says, is not the meaning: the point is only that the generation which had long been rebellious was now dead, and that it was therefore a fit time for God to regard the miseries of the posterity. Keil and Delitzsch grant the great truth here, since the fall of the kingdom was owed to the sins of earlier generations, but warn that the truth becomes error if the speakers are taken to think themselves innocent, which they contradict later by confessing that they have sinned. Ellicott says the same, that the complaint is that the earlier offenders had passed away without the punishment which now fell on their descendants, who thus bore a double penalty. Clarke settles it by a distinction, that nations as such cannot be punished in another world, so that national judgments must fall in this life, and that this is the only way in which children bear the sins of their fathers.
8:
Who the servants were is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch reject four identifications, the soldiers of the invading army, the invaders as lately subject to an older empire, their governors as officers of a king, and slaves set over the captives; they take the word of the conquerors, called servants partly for the despotism under which the people were placed and partly because these ought rather to have served them had they been faithful. Ellicott gives it a courtly turn, that insult was added to injury by sending as rulers men who had filled menial offices at court; Clarke leans to the soldiers, quoting a Latin line asking what masters may do where slaves have grown so insolent. Calvin makes the degradation itself the point: it is no shame to serve a king, and a servitude that does not look degrading is thought tolerable, but to become the servants of servants wounds the mind most grievously, and the more so in a people that had been a priestly kingdom.

The bread got at the peril of life produces the sharpest disagreement here, and it turns on one word. Calvin observes that the noun means drought as well as sword, and since the passage is about famine and desert he has no doubt drought is meant; he wonders that the sense of sword occurred to anybody, asking what a sword has to do with a wilderness. On his reading the phrase means the barrenness of the desert, the want by which the people were distressed. The rest keep the sword. Keil and Delitzsch identify it with the predatory Bedouins of the desert, who fell on those bringing in bread and plundered and probably killed them, and they reject both the view that the bread was fetched from neighbouring countries and the view that it was wrung from the plunderers, referring it to the ingathering of a scanty harvest in a devastated country. Ellicott says the same of nomad tribes attacking the gleaners, and Clarke that they could not go out to feed cattle without being harassed by marauding parties. Gill refers the verse to the siege, when men slipped privately out of the city for provisions.

The colour of the skin divides them again. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the verb means to be blackened and give it the sense of being kindled or made to glow, since the word for oven denotes the fire burning in it rather than any blackness on it; their rendering is that the skin glows like a baker oven, a strong expression for the fever-heat produced by hunger. Ellicott agrees, preferring fiery red and rendering the second phrase the fever-blast of famine, and says the words paint the hot fever of hunger rather than the livid paleness of exhaustion. Calvin keeps the blackness and supports it from a psalm that speaks of lying among the pots and being deformed by blackness; his account is that the famine left no moisture in them, and that from paleness came a greater deformity and blackness. Gill agrees, adding the burning winds frequent in warmer countries, and Clarke the searching winds that burnt up every green thing.

On the outrage in the city Calvin notes that the word used is a delicate one for a disgraceful act, and builds the aggravation on the place. The city is named by its holy mountain, a part put for the whole, but that was the place chosen for the worship of the name of God and so his earthly dwelling; such things done there were not merely disgraceful but a profanation of that worship, and so sacrilege. Gill reaches the same point, that the deed was more abominable for being done on the holy mountain, and adds that it was done by the servants just spoken of, and not in the land of exile but at the taking of the city.
12:
How the princes were hanged is read three ways, the boldest reading being Calvin. Everyone else translates that they were slain by the hand of their enemies, and he wonders that it never occurred to them that a far more grievous thing is meant, that they perished by their own. To say that princes were hanged by an enemy would be frigid, since it was common enough for the conquered to be killed and hung up by way of reproach; that they were driven to lay violent hands on themselves is far more atrocious, and no more incredible than the earlier report of tender women devouring their children. He concedes that the most obvious sense is suspension by the hand rather than the neck, a punishment not recorded as practised then. Gill canvasses the same three and prefers the last, if an instance so early could be produced.

Clarke has no doubt of it: they were suspended from hooks in the wall by their hands until torture and exhaustion killed them, and left to be devoured by the birds, as the body of a king was once fastened to a city wall. Ellicott takes the verse of exposure after death rather than of execution, and observes that neither age nor dignity, both implied in the word for elders, was any safeguard in life or death.

The grinding is a question of what was carried. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the phrase means they were taken for the mill, since there is no ground for it in the language and it does not suit the parallelism; the noun is the mill, and to bear it means to work at it and with it. They have in view the portable hand-mill found in every household, and take the carrying of the mill, not merely of the upper stone, as the heaviest part of the labour. Ellicott reads it the same way, adding that the young men carried the mill itself, probably as they marched with the armies toward Babylon, while the striplings of the next clause carried firewood and literally staggered under it. Clarke notes that this was the work of female slaves, and Calvin that of all servile employments it was the lowest. Calvin also rejects an old rendering which made the young men basely abused, since the word means to grind or to tear and the second half of the verse will not bear it.

The gate draws the most interesting comment. Keil and Delitzsch insist it was not only where public affairs were deliberated but a place of social entertainment, since there were no refreshment rooms or public baths such as are now found in those countries, and a place for watching the motley multitude of passers-by; the parallel clause about music proves, they argue, that entertainment and not only justice is meant. Ellicott says the same, that the gate served for counsel and judgment and also for social converse, the music here and the dancing next marking a like interruption of the joys of the young. Clarke reads only the loss of justice, the people being under military law. Calvin combines both: men cannot dwell together without laws and courts, and where courts are closed barbarity prevails, which is worse than solitude, while where there are no assemblies for legitimate amusements life becomes brutal, since man is a sociable being. He adds that the desolation followed them into exile, since they were dispersed deliberately so that they should not combine, the design being to obliterate the name of the people.

On the last verse Gill notices that the verb has the sense of keeping sabbath, an allusion to the joy once expressed on their festivals. Calvin corrects the rendering, since the word means not dancing but playing on a pipe, and closes with the observation that life is more bitter than death where men are in constant mourning.
16:
What the fallen crown stands for is taken broadly. Gill makes it the whole honour of the nation, the glory of kingdom and priesthood, and reports two narrower readings, referring it to the temple or to the garlands worn at feasts. Clarke takes the festal sense, since at feasts and marriages they crowned themselves with flowers and all such festivity was at an end, and allows the loss of sovereignty as well. Ellicott declines to narrow it, calling the phrase naturally symbolic of degradation and holding that it need not be restricted either to the destruction of the temple or the devastation of the city. Calvin combines the two: the crown covers all the ornaments with which the people had been adorned, the kingdom and the priesthood being like two precious jewels, and a crown was besides a symbol of joy and honour, worn not by kings only but at weddings and feasts.

The confession that follows is where the chapter answers itself. Ellicott points out that this acknowledgment of personal sin contrasts with the half-complaining tone of the verse about the fathers. Calvin makes the same connection and treats it as decisive: when he said that the fathers who sinned were dead and their iniquity borne by the children, he did not exempt the living, for here he condemns them and includes himself. The purpose of the exclamation, he adds, is not to exasperate their sorrow but to humble them into perceiving that the punishment is just, as though they were summoned before a tribunal.

On the fainting heart and the dimmed eyes Keil and Delitzsch find the halves unmistakeably parallel, the sickening of the heart answering to the dimness of the eyes as the sorrow of the soul answers to its expression in tears. Ellicott distributes the two demonstratives, the first pointing to the loss of national honour just named and the second to the horrors recited before it. Calvin defends the intensity of the grief, since their afflictions were not ordinary; and he explains the dimness as the effect of grief, which blunts the senses so that the sight is injured.

Henry finds here the thing that hurt most. The people express a deeper concern for the ruins of the temple than for any other calamity; for other desolations, he says, their hearts grieve and their eyes weep, but for this their hearts faint and their eyes are dim. From that he draws the note that nothing lies so heavily on the spirits of good people as what threatens the ruin of religion, and that it is a comfort if we can appeal to God that this afflicts us more than any affliction of our own. He adds the justice of it, that the people had polluted the mountain and God made it desolate, so that the beasts walk there as freely as in the woods. Gill says the same, that the loss of their civil interest did not affect them as the interest of religion did.

Calvin gives the desolation of the mountain its full weight. That place had been chosen by God as though he had come down from heaven to dwell there; the change is therefore not merely sad but monstrous, that where God had dwelt beasts should lodge as in a deserted cave and succeed in the place of God and of the faithful. He notes that the verse may be joined to the one before it or taken by itself. Clarke observes that the animals are numerous there and that desolated land was always reckoned the resort of wild beasts, as happens anywhere once the inhabitants are removed, while Ellicott would render the word jackals haunting the ruins. Keil and Delitzsch mark the hinge here, that the glory of the earthly habitation is at an end while the throne of the Lord endures for ever, so that the lamentation rises into prayer.
19:
The turn from complaint to prayer rests on the permanence of God. Gill lists the respects in which he remains the same, in nature and perfections, in grace and goodness, in purpose and promise, and makes the contrast sharp: though his own sanctuary lay in ruins, he continued just as he ever was. He adds that the eternity of God is of great comfort in times of distress. Clarke turns the same fact into petition, that since God suffers no change and once loved them, that love may be renewed. Ellicott takes the verb literally as sitting, which the next clause shows to mean upon a throne, and finds the comfort in the unchangeableness of his purpose of love.

Calvin makes the verse a lesson in where to look. The prophet raises his eyes to God and encourages the godly to do the same whatever their calamities; and Calvin compares a psalm on the same ruin, composed, he thinks, while the people were already in exile, in which the heavens grow old and waste away with the whole world, and then the same acclamation follows. He observes that the psalm is the clearer, since it applies the doctrine expressly to the consolation of the church, promising that the children of the servants of God shall inhabit the land, and so infers the perpetuity of the church from the perpetuity of God; our prophet does not draw that inference, though Calvin holds it implied. His own application is a rule about vision: while we fix our eyes on present things we must vacillate, since nothing in the world is permanent, and when adversity clouds the eyes faith in a manner vanishes; the remedy is to raise the eyes to God, who remains the same though the world should perish a hundred times.

The question that follows is an expostulation. Ellicott calls it the problem of the mystery of suffering, then as at all times, God having seemed forgetful and indifferent to their miseries. Gill explains the appearance rather than the fact, that God seems to forget when he does not arise immediately, and that a deferred deliverance looks like an eternity to those waiting. Calvin allows the expostulation and defends it: the faithful, even while they patiently bear their evils, familiarly deposit their complaints in the bosom of God, as David both prayed and expostulated in the same breath; and in taking that liberty they do not put off reverence or humility.

Calvin adds the observation that most repays attention. When the prophet asks why God should forget for ever, he was relying on his own prophecies and deferring his hope to the end of the seventy years already prefixed; the complaint of length was made according to human judgment. Calvin thinks the form was composed to outlast its author, dictated so that the faithful might use it after his death; and he adds the caution that when we pray so we should remember that our times are in the hand of God.

Keil and Delitzsch record a liturgical fact about the end of the book. In many manuscripts the next verse is repeated after the last, so that the poem may not close with the mention of the wrath of God, the same thing being done at the end of three other books, the intention being to conclude with comfort. They hold that the last verse, rightly understood, never required it, and quote an older commentator to the effect that the writer did not speak as one despairing of the salvation of his people but only to make plain his grief. That agrees, they say, with the character of the whole work, in which complaint and supplication continue to the end, though not without hope; and they borrow a phrase for it, that the hope glimmers from afar, like the morning star through clouds.
21:
The kind of turning asked for divides Gill from Calvin. Gill takes the petition of repentance, as expressing their sense of backsliding and their inability to turn themselves; he will not confine it to a return to the land, but understands it of a turning of the heart and a reformation of the life. Calvin says expressly that repentance is not what is spoken of, and distinguishes an inward turning, when God regenerates men by his Spirit, from an outward turning on his own part, when he so receives them into favour that his paternal kindness becomes apparent. It is the last that the verse asks. Ellicott stands between them: a man could not turn himself and re-establish the old filial relation, but he could ask God to turn him, and felt that such a prayer would not be asked in vain. Clarke reads it of restoration outright, that they might regain their country, their temple and the offices of their religion, and above all the divine favour.

Calvin uses the clause to say something about the ground of hope. The remedy lies in the hand of God whenever he pleases to help, and this is not confidence but its beginning; for despair weakens us so that we cannot call on God at all, because we think it is over with us, and we think so because we confine his power and by unbelief repel it. It is therefore the beginning of hope to believe that all the issues of death are in his hand, and that though we were swallowed up a hundred times he could become the author of salvation at any moment.

The last verse has been read four ways. Gill states the difficulty first, that the words look as though the petitioners had no hope of being heard; and he offers three escapes, rendering it though thou hast in rejecting rejected us, or unless thou hast utterly rejected us, or best of all as a question, wilt thou utterly reject us, to which the answer is that such goodness surely will not. Ellicott reaches the same result by the second: the received version makes the mourner fall back from a hopeful prayer into despair, whereas the word should be rendered unless, so that utter rejection is named only as the one thing that could prevent renewal, and named as impossible; God has not rejected, and therefore he will renew.

Clarke lays out the alternatives without settling on one. His own paraphrase keeps the appearance of finality, that it seems as though their reprobation were sealed; and he answers it from history rather than grammar, since the prayer was heard and at the end of seventy years they were restored. He then reports a scholar who insists the particle is causal and renders it that God has surely cast them off altogether, the rejection being the ground of the petition that precedes; and another who holds that no good sense can be made of the place unless it is read as a question.

Calvin rejects one reading and is candid about the motive behind it. Some divide the verse and render it that surely if God has rejected them he is very angry; Calvin calls this forced, and thinks those who adopted it were driven to pervert the words because it seemed hard to say that the people had been wholly rejected. Offended by that harshness, they contrived the comment; he prefers with most interpreters to take the particles adversatively.

Clarke closes with what the copies do. He quotes an old English rendering of the previous verse asking that their days be renewed as in old time, because they have been banished long enough; and he adds that in one of his oldest manuscripts the twenty-first verse is repeated at the end of the twenty-second, and that in another older still only its first word stands there.
